**When "Better" Isn't Really Better: The Hidden Traps of A/B Testing**

A/B testing sounds simple: show version A to one group, show version B to another, and pick the winner. In practice, however, many companies make decisions based on flawed tests without realizing it. Understanding the methodology behind A/B testing is what separates reliable insights from expensive mistakes.

The foundation of any A/B test is the control group and the treatment group. The control group sees the existing experience — the baseline. The treatment group sees the new version you want to evaluate. For the test to be valid, users must be assigned to groups randomly. Without randomization, you cannot be sure that differences in outcomes are caused by your change rather than by pre-existing differences between the groups.

One of the most common mistakes in A/B testing is called **peeking**. This happens when a data scientist checks results before the planned end date and stops the test early because the numbers look good. The problem is statistical: the more often you check, the higher the probability of seeing a false positive. Imagine flipping a coin ten times and getting seven heads. You might think the coin is biased. But if you keep flipping, the results often balance out. Early stopping creates the same illusion.

Sample size is another critical factor. Before launching a test, you need to calculate how many users are required to detect a meaningful difference. This calculation depends on three things: the minimum detectable effect (how small a change you care about), the significance level (typically 5%), and statistical power (typically 80%). If your sample is too small, you risk a **Type II error** — failing to detect a real improvement. Many teams skip this step and end up with inconclusive results that waste time and resources.

Consider a real-world scenario: an e-commerce company tests a new checkout button color. After three days, the conversion rate for the green button is 2.1% versus 1.9% for the blue one. The team celebrates and ships the change. But the test ran for only 500 sessions per group. The required sample size for that effect size was 4,000 per group. The observed difference was almost certainly due to random variation, not the button color.

Finally, it is important to choose the right **primary metric** before the test begins. Teams that define success after seeing results are vulnerable to **metric shopping** — unconsciously selecting whichever metric looks best. A good practice is to pre-register your hypothesis: document what you expect to improve and how you will measure it, before collecting any data.

A/B testing is one of the most powerful tools in a data scientist's toolkit. But its power comes only when the methodology is applied with discipline and rigor.
